clue.text: "It falls to my lot ", to quote the successful purchaser

definitions.text: "It falls to my lot ", to quote the successful purchaser

parts.words: "It falls to my lot ", to quote the successful purchaser
parts.note: at an auction the gavel comes down on each lot as it is sold, so the bidder who wins could say it has fallen to him

explanation.surface: A buyer boasts about his good fortune in winning something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lot' reads as one's fate, but it is an item for sale at auction, and what 'falls' is the auctioneer's gavel.
explanation.definitionFit: The auctioneer's mallet is brought down to mark the sale of each lot.

parts.note: Harpo, one of the Marx Brothers, played the stringed instrument whose name also means to nag repeatedly

explanation.surface: A Marx brother went on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marx' suggests Karl, but it is Harpo Marx, who played the harp; to 'harp on' is to keep on about something.
explanation.definitionFit: Harpo Marx was a player of the harp, the instrument whose name also means to nag.

parts.note: points to the hat-maker who presides over the tea-party in Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: Someone runs a book club's afternoon gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary tea-party' sounds like a book-group event; it is the famous tea-party in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's eccentric milliner hosts the tea-party with the March Hare.

clue.text: The old thing comes up after a time with the rubber

indicators.note: after places the second piece behind the first

parts.note: an era is a period of time

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: res is the Latin, and old legal, word for a thing

explanation.surface: An antique turns up some time later along with an india-rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes up' works because this is a down clue, so the reversed word reads upwards. 'The old thing' is Latin, the language of old law terms; 'rubber' is British for a pencil eraser, not a tyre or condom.
explanation.definitionFit: An india-rubber is used to erase pencil marks.

indicators.note: to perform is to act out or work over, so the preceding letters are put through a routine and come out rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written: the British Overseas Airways Corporation, the old national airline

explanation.surface: The headline turns at an airline's in-flight entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: Old-style &lit: the letters of STAR and BOAC rearrange to give the answer, and the whole clue describes star performers who tumble. BOAC was Britain's long-haul state airline.
explanation.definitionFit: Tumblers and trapeze artists are leading circus performers.

parts.note: the word for a cheek or jaw is also the first part of ... and ..., the pedlar who sold such books, and means a fellow

explanation.surface: An impertinent bookseller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' reads as impudent but means to do with the cheek: the word means a jaw or cheek, a fellow, and begins 'chapbook'.
explanation.definitionFit: A word meaning a cheek or jaw, and a man, as in a chapman selling books.

clue.text: A flower with love to a swimmer

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit Hero in Greek legend

explanation.surface: Someone presents a bloom to a lover who swims.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander is the youth of Greek myth who swam across the Hellespont to meet Hero.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mediterranean evergreen shrub grown for its pink or white blooms.

clue.text: "The moving moon went up the sky And no where did 99" (Coleridge)

definitions.text: "The moving moon went up the sky And no where did 99" (Coleridge)

parts.words: "The moving moon went up the sky And no where did 99" (Coleridge)
parts.note: fill the gap in the line from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, where the moon never stays still

explanation.surface: A line about the moon's journey across the night sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The 99 is the OCR of the printed dash marking the gap. The line from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner continues 'Softly she was going up'.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb in Coleridge's line means to stay or remain in one place.

clue.text: It may get in one's eyes, motes and all

definitions.text: It may get in one's eyes, motes and all

parts.words: It may get in one's eyes, motes and all
parts.note: a shaft of light shows floating dust specks, recalling the Gospel saying about the mote in another's eye and the beam in one's own

explanation.surface: Something dazzles a person, dust specks included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motes' recalls the Sermon on the Mount's mote and beam; here the beam is a shaft of sunlight in which motes of dust dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A ray of daylight that can dazzle, often showing drifting dust.

clue.text: Though strict in his arrest he's not necessarily a sergeant !

definitions.text: Though strict in his arrest he's not necessarily a sergeant !

parts.words: Though strict in his arrest he's not necessarily a sergeant
parts.note: the clue describes a soldier serving as a military policeman, nicknamed after the scarlet top of his headgear, who makes arrests whatever his rank

explanation.surface: A stern arresting officer may hold a lowly rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrest' looks like the subject's own detention but is the arrests he makes. In Britain a military policeman is nicknamed for the scarlet cover on his cap; 'sergeant' plays on the common phrase about sergeants and police.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a British military policeman, from the scarlet cap cover they wear.

clue.text: The Emperor has the remedy for all ills !

definitions.meaning: a third-century Roman emperor, captured by the Persians
a herb whose root was taken as a sedative, long called all-heal

explanation.surface: A ruler is credited with a cure for everything.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a Roman ruler, and also of a medicinal plant traditionally known as all-heal.

parts.note: a young wild duck still learning to fly is called by the same name as a lively 1920s young woman

explanation.surface: A girl is affectionately called a little duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like an endearment for a girl, but a young duckling beating its wings is also known by the name of the 1920s good-time girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashionable young woman of the 1920s, and a young duck not yet able to fly.

clue.text: Without sex appeal she's liable to get confused

indicators.note: here 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, so one piece goes around the other
being confused jumbles the word before it into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman lacking allure is prone to becoming muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but is its old sense 'outside': the scrambled word ('to get confused') goes round the abbreviation. 'She's' stands for the definition 'she', a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so it can stand for any female person referred to.

clue.text: Due to high pollen count in a ring of roses ?

definitions.text: Due to high pollen count in a ring of roses ?

parts.words: Due to high pollen count in a ring of roses
parts.note: the nursery rhyme about a ring of roses ends with everyone going 'atishoo', which hay fever from pollen also causes

explanation.surface: Pollen in a circle of flowers causes trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring a ring o' roses' is a children's singing game whose verse ends 'Atishoo! Atishoo! We all fall down'; read literally, a ring of real roses would provoke the same reaction.
explanation.definitionFit: An involuntary blast of air through the nose, the typical hay-fever response.

clue.text: "——! The very word is like a bell" (Keats)

definitions.text: The very word is like a bell" (Keats)

parts.words: The very word is like a bell" (Keats)
parts.note: the opening of the last stanza of the Ode to a Nightingale, where the poet repeats the word that ended the previous stanza

explanation.surface: A poet hears a single word ring out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Keats's Ode to a Nightingale the seventh stanza ends 'faery lands forlorn', and the eighth begins by repeating that word, which tolls him back to himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective Keats repeats means abandoned and desolate.

definitions.meaning: to lug or haul something along
the betting system pooling all stakes, run in Britain by a body known by a short name for the totalisator

explanation.surface: Someone lugs the betting pool around.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb for hauling a load, and the short name for the totalisator betting pool.

parts.note: swapping the opening sounds of 'well-boiled icicle' gives 'well-oiled bicycle', the kind of slip Rev. Spooner was famous for

explanation.surface: A frozen icicle somehow boiled for a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is nonsense until its initial sounds are exchanged: B moves from 'boiled' to 'icicle', giving a well-oiled bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip of the tongue exchanging initial sounds, named after an Oxford don.

parts.note: Boniface, the landlord in Farquhar's play The Beaux' Stratagem, became a byword for a publican, and the phrase also reads as one who keeps in

explanation.surface: A man named Boniface never leaves the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Boniface is the landlord in George Farquhar's comedy The Beaux' Stratagem; 'stay-at-home' splits the answer as one who keeps in.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord of a hostelry, the trade of Farquhar's Boniface.

parts.note: a gull is a dupe or easy mark, so one who catches gulls is a cheat

explanation.definitionFit: A gull is a credulous person, and a cheat is one who dupes such people.

parts.note: tumblers at 4 across perform sideways handsprings, which share their name with a broad-brimmed hat

explanation.surface: Somebody fashions peculiar hats for a troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headgear' points to hats, and a wide-brimmed hat is indeed called this; but the 'odd headgear' is the acrobats' way of going head over heels sideways.
explanation.definitionFit: Sideways handsprings are a stock acrobatic move; the same word names a wide-brimmed hat.

clue.text: "And his —— were gleaming in purple and gold" (Byron)

definitions.text: "And his —— were gleaming in purple and gold" (Byron)

parts.words: "And his —— were gleaming in purple and gold" (Byron)
parts.note: fill the gap in the second line of The Destruction of Sennacherib, describing the Assyrian army

explanation.surface: A line about an army shining in royal colours.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's poem opens 'The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold, And his ... were gleaming in purple and gold'.
explanation.definitionFit: Divisions of soldiers, as in the Roman army, here Sennacherib's troops.

parts.note: reads like inventing a story, but means working wool into a garment with needles

explanation.surface: Someone invents a tall story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make up a yarn' suggests storytelling; here the yarn is wool being made up into fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Working wool with needles makes it up into a garment.

parts.note: the nursery rhyme runs 'Born on a Monday, christened on' the day that follows

explanation.surface: A man's christening day is asked about.
explanation.walkthrough: Solomon Grundy is a nursery-rhyme character: 'Born on a Monday, christened on Tuesday, married on Wednesday...'.
explanation.definitionFit: The second weekday, when the rhyme's Solomon Grundy was christened.

parts.note: traps and nooses share their name with the drums whose wires rattle against the skin

explanation.definitionFit: Traps for catching animals, and also side drums with rattling wires across them.

parts.note: 'puss' is an old country name for the hare, and dashing away fast is named after that animal

explanation.surface: A cat bolts away quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puss' suggests a cat, but it is a traditional name for a hare, and running off like one is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rushing away very fast, as a startled hare does.

parts.note: red was the colour of the Soviet Russians
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A Russian treatise on defensive works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' reads as a piece of writing but is the grammatical article AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A field work with two faces forming a salient angle.

clue.text: You'll see me errant among the rovers!

definitions.text: You'll see me errant among the rovers!

indicators.note: rovers wander about, so the letters given here roam into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wandering knight joins a band of travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: Old-style &lit: ME ERRANT rearranges to give the answer, a Merseyside town whose football club is called the Rovers.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on the Wirral whose football club plays as the Rovers.

parts.note: un- is a prefix meaning not
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone out of touch with fashion is remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not with it' reads as unfashionable, but it splits into a negative prefix joined to the plain word; 'That's singular' means 'that which is single'.
explanation.definitionFit: A single thing or one, which is what is meant by something singular.

clue.text: It's fragrant to look back in somewhat tender association

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the middle of the other
somewhat signals the word that follows is only roughly as written, its letters altered
an association brings letters together in a new grouping
back says the short word is turned round

parts.note: LO is an old word meaning look, as in 'lo and behold'

explanation.surface: Something smells sweet when one fondly recalls a past connection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns the old word for 'look', and 'in' places it inside the rearranged letters; the anagram is signalled by two words, 'somewhat' and 'association', either side of 'tender'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something giving off a pleasant smell.

clue.text: One yard of seating at Delphi ?

definitions.text: One yard of seating at Delphi ?

parts.words: One yard of seating at Delphi
parts.note: a yard is three feet, and the priestess at Delphi sat on a three-legged stool to give oracles

explanation.surface: A short bench in a Greek stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One yard' is a length, but read as three feet it describes a three-legged seat like the one the Delphic oracle used.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-legged stand or stool, like the seat of the Delphic priestess.

parts.note: can read as a good, reliable quality, but refers to the richness of a tone

explanation.definitionFit: Resonance or fullness of tone is what the word describes.

clue.text: Bird that gets an outsize victim

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
a hunted victim is prey

explanation.surface: A bird catches a creature far bigger than usual.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish-eating hawk, a bird of prey.
